l1-basics: Texas Hold'em is the world's most popular poker variant. Each player receives 2 hole cards and combines them with 5 community cards to make the best 5-card hand and win the pot.
Core goal: not to win every hand, but to make +EV (positive expected value) decisions over the long run.

1. Preflop: each player gets 2 hole cards, action starts after the blinds post
2. Flop: 3 community cards are dealt
3. Turn: the 4th community card is dealt
4. River: the 5th community card is dealt
5. Showdown: reveal hands and compare
Royal Flush > Straight Flush > Four of a Kind > Full House > Flush > Straight > Three of a Kind > Two Pair > One Pair > High Card
Remember: Flush beats Straight! Many beginners mix up this order.
Pro players calculate probabilities on every hand. Building the habit of asking "what's my equity here?" is your first step toward playing professionally.

Total starting-hand combinations: C(52,2) = 52×51÷2 = 1326
Pocket pairs (e.g. AA): C(4,2) = 6
Suited hands (e.g. AKs): 4
Offsuit hands (e.g. AKo): 12

Understanding these basic combinatorics is the foundation of range analysis — the pot-odds math and Blocker effects you'll learn later all build on it.

Theory reference: the full derivation of combinatorics and starting-hand probability is in Theory Academy T1 Chapter 1 "Combinatorics and Starting-Hand Probability" — covering the C(n,k) formula, the origin of the 1326 combinations, and the 6/4/12 atomic units.

Counter-intuitive: 169 classes and 1326 combinations are two different counts. 169 is the number of "equivalent classes" (pair/suited/offsuit types), while 1326 is the number of "distinguishable actual combinations". Probability math must use 1326 — classes deceive you: suited AK and AA each count as "1 class", but their combination weights are 4 and 6 respectively.
l1-position: In Texas Hold'em, position refers to where you sit at the table relative to the dealer button. Players acting later have a huge advantage because they can see the actions of everyone before them before deciding.
Golden rule: the button (BTN) is the best position — you act last and have the most information.

Early: UTG, UTG+1 — act first with the least information, need the strongest hands
Middle: MP, HJ — middle positions, can widen slightly
Late: CO, BTN — act late with the most information, widest range
Blinds: SB, BB — have chips committed, but act first postflop
The same hand is worth far more on the BTN than in UTG. For example, KJo is a standard open on the BTN but should usually fold in UTG — UTG opens only the very strongest slice of hands.
Pro players strictly adjust their starting-hand range by position. Only a few hands (AA/KK/QQ/AKs) are playable "in any position"; everything else must be adjusted by position.

1. Preflop: late position can steal blinds and open a wider range
2. Postflop: late position controls pot size and makes more precise value bets
3. Information edge: decide after seeing opponents' actions, reducing error rate

The exact composition and mixing frequencies of every position's range are defined by the Range Trainer module and the GTO strategy chart (the single source of truth for preflop).

Relative opening width by position:
UTG opens only the very strongest slice of hands, HJ slightly wider, CO noticeably wider (nearly 30%), the BTN is the widest opening position at a 6-max table (about 35%), and the SB is in the same tier as the BTN (about 35%).

Equity realization: the BTN has position postflop and realizes its equity better; UTG is out of position postflop, realizing only about 80-90%.

Rule: the later your position, the wider you may open and the better your postflop equity realization — but the width steps between adjacent positions are not uniform: they stay tight up front and only widen markedly at CO/BTN.

Theory reference: quantitative analysis of position value is in Theory Academy T3 Chapter 1 "Position Value and Equity Realization"; the modern revision of the Gap Concept is in T3 Chapter 2; Sklansky's Fundamental Theorem is in T3 Chapter 3.

Counter-intuitive: BTN's positional advantage is mainly postflop, not preflop. Preflop BTN only acts last; but postflop BTN acts last on every street — meaning you can see all opponents' actions before deciding, which is a huge information advantage.
l1-hand-selection: Starting-hand selection is the most fundamental and important skill in Texas Hold'em. Playing too many hands (too loose) or too few (too tight) seriously hurts your win rate.
The most common beginner mistake: playing too many hands. In 6-max, you should only play about 20-25% of hands.

Tier 1 (playable in any position): AA, KK, QQ, AKs
Tier 2 (playable from middle position on): JJ, TT, AQs, AQo, AJs
Tier 3 (playable from late position/blinds): 99-22, KQs, KJs, QJs, JTs, T9s, 98s
Garbage (fold in any position): unsuited small hands like 72o, 83o, 94o
s = suited, o = offsuit. Suited hands are worth about 3-4% more than offsuit hands.

1. High-card value: A/K/Q/J combinations are stronger
2. Connectivity: connected cards (e.g. JTs) have straight potential
3. Suitedness: suited cards have flush potential
4. Domination: avoid easily dominated hands (e.g. K3o vs KQo)

Pro players' starting ranges are far tighter than recreational players'. Better to play fewer good hands than to lose big chips in marginal spots. Discipline is one of the most important qualities of a professional player.

Starting-hand combinatorics (atomic units):
Any pocket pair (e.g. AA) = C(4,2) = 6 combinations
Any suited hand (e.g. AKs) = 4 combinations
Any offsuit hand (e.g. AKo) = 4×4-4 = 12 combinations
Any two different ranks = 16 combinations

Probability of any pocket pair = 78/1326 ≈ 5.9% (about once every 17 hands)
Probability of AA = 6/1326 ≈ 0.45% (about once every 221 hands)
Theory reference: starting-hand probability and combinatorics are detailed in Theory Academy T1 Chapter 1. The relationship between starting-hand EV tiers and position is in T3 Chapter 1.

Counter-intuitive: AKs has only 4 combinations while AA has 6. Although AK looks the most "imposing", its combination weight is lower than a pocket pair's. In range analysis, pairs in an opponent's 3-Bet range usually outweigh AK in combination weight — a quantitative bias many beginners overlook.
l1-bankroll: Why Is Bankroll Management So Important?
Bankroll management is the foundation of every successful poker player. No matter how good your skills are, without sound bankroll management, variance will eventually bankrupt you.
Golden rule: never sit at a table with more than 5% of your total bankroll. For cash games, keep 20-30 buy-ins; for tournaments, keep 50-100 buy-ins.

Cash game NL10 (BB $0.10):
  Minimum: 20 × $10 = $200
  Recommended: 30 × $10 = $300

Cash game NL50 (BB $0.50):
  Minimum: 20 × $50 = $1,000
  Recommended: 30 × $50 = $1,500

Tournament $11 buy-in:
  Minimum: 50 × $11 = $550
  Recommended: 100 × $11 = $1,100

When your bankroll grows to the next stake's standard line, you can try moving up:
• Move up: bankroll reaches 30 buy-ins of the higher stake
• Move down: bankroll drops below 20 buy-ins of the current stake
• Moving down isn't shameful — protecting your bankroll is what long-term winners do
Completely separate your poker bankroll from living expenses. Never play with money you "can't afford to lose", because it seriously damages your decision quality.

Kelly Criterion (optimal betting fraction in bankroll management):
f* = (bp - q) / b
where f* = optimal bankroll fraction, b = odds (net odds), p = win probability, q = loss probability = 1-p

Cash game requirement: 20-30 buy-ins (minimum-recommended)
Tournament requirement: 50-100 buy-ins (minimum-recommended)

Example: NL10 table, each buy-in $10, recommended bankroll = 30 × $10 = $300

Theory reference: the quantitative model of bankroll management and the Kelly Criterion in poker are covered in Theory Academy T8 Chapter 2 "Bankroll Psychology and Quantitative Management", which fully covers poker psychology's bankroll management methodology.
l1-leaks: Why Is Identifying Errors More Important Than Learning Techniques?
Fixing one error usually gains more than learning one new technique. Here are the 10 most common beginner leaks, ordered from most severe to least:
Leak #1: Playing Too Many Hands (VPIP Too High)

Beginners are usually involved in 40-60% of deals, while winning players keep it to about 20-25%.

How to fix: stick strictly to your preflop ranges (the Range Trainer and the GTO strategy tables are the source of truth for each position's exact composition and frequencies) — only play hands worth playing.

Playing too many hands from bad position and ignoring positional advantage.

Fix: UTG and HJ open only the very strongest slice of hands, CO widens noticeably (nearly 30%), and the BTN is the widest opening position at a 6-max table (about 35%). The exact composition of each position's range is defined by the Range Trainer module and the GTO strategy chart.
Leak #3: Passive Calling (Too Many Calls, Too Few Raises)
"Call is the weakest action" — most of the time you should raise or fold instead of passively calling.

Betting too small lets opponents call easily; betting too big wastes what a small bet could achieve.

Standard: 1/3-2/3 pot on the flop, 2/3-full pot on the turn/river.

#5 Not tracking pot size (can't calculate odds)
#6 Continuing to play after tilting
#7 Unbalanced bluffing frequency (either never bluffing or bluffing too much)
#8 Ignoring opponent behavior patterns
#9 Not reviewing hands
#10 No stop-loss or time limits
Each Leak you fix may raise your win rate by 1-3 BB/100. Fixing the first 5 Leaks can turn you from a loser into a winner.
Focus on one Leak per week rather than fixing everything at once. Track your progress with a check-in calendar.

Theory reference: the mathematical essence behind common Leaks is a missing EV decision framework. The full definition and derivation of expected value is in Theory Academy T2 Chapter 1 "Expected Value (EV): The Unified Measure of All Decisions". Once you understand EV, every Leak can be quantified as a repeating pattern of -EV behavior.

Counter-intuitive: a decision that often loses can still be correct. EV only guarantees long-run average profit; single results are governed by variance. A +EV call can lose 10 times in a row — the EV of the 11th call is still positive. Pro players focus on decision quality, not single outcomes.

l1-basics-q1.question: Which hand is the strongest?
l1-basics-q1.explanation: Four of a Kind > Full House > Flush > Straight

l1-basics-q2.question: How many community cards are dealt on the Flop?
l1-basics-q2.explanation: The flop deals 3 community cards, the turn 1, and the river 1 — 5 in total.

l1-basics-q3.question: What is the core goal in Texas Hold'em?
options: Make +EV decisions over the long run
l1-basics-q3.explanation: Pro players care about long-term expected value (EV), not single-hand results.

l1-pos-q1.question: Which position is the best?
l1-pos-q1.explanation: BTN (button) is the best position — you almost always act last with the most information.

l1-pos-q2.question: What should you do with KJo in UTG?
l1-pos-q2.explanation: KJo in UTG is a marginal hand (right at the upper edge of the UTG opening range); modern strategy allows a loose open, but conservative play still suggests folding.

l1-pos-q3.question: What is the biggest advantage of late position?
l1-pos-q3.explanation: Late position's biggest advantage is information — you decide after seeing all previous actions.

l1-hand-q1.question: In 6-max, what's the ideal VPIP?
l1-hand-q1.explanation: In 6-max you should only play about 20-25% of hands. Playing too many hands is the most common beginner mistake.

l1-hand-q2.question: Which hand can open-raise from UTG?
l1-hand-q2.explanation: AJs (suited Ace-Jack) is strong enough to open standard from UTG. K8o and 76o are too weak, and QJo isn't strong enough from early position.

l1-hand-q3.question: What does "s" mean in AKs?
l1-hand-q3.explanation: s = suited, meaning both cards are the same suit. AKs is a suited Ace and King.

l1-bankroll-q1.question: How much bankroll is the recommended minimum for NL10 cash games?
l1-bankroll-q1.explanation: 20 buy-ins × $10/buy-in = $200 is the minimum; $300 (30 buy-ins) is recommended.

l1-bankroll-q2.question: When should you move down?
options: When the bankroll drops below 20 buy-ins of the current stake
l1-bankroll-q2.explanation: Moving down should be based on objective bankroll standards, not emotions. Move down to protect capital when under-rolled.

l1-bankroll-q3.question: Which of these is wrong?
options: Separate poker bankroll from living expenses
l1-bankroll-q3.explanation: Borrowing money to chase losses is the most dangerous practice — it leads to tilt and bigger losses.

l1-leaks-q1.question: What VPIP range do winning players typically have?
l1-leaks-q1.explanation: Winning 6-max players typically run a VPIP around 20-25%, varying by position and style.

l1-leaks-q2.question: Which of these is NOT a common beginner mistake?
l1-leaks-q2.explanation: Strictly following range charts is correct — not a mistake.

l1-leaks-q3.question: What is the standard flop bet size?
l1-leaks-q3.explanation: The standard flop bet is 1/3 to 2/3 of the pot, adjusted by board texture and range advantage.

l1-basics-ex1.title: Identify the hand: Flush vs Straight
reasoning: You hold 8♥9♥ and the board shows T♥J♥2♥
You make an 8-9-T-J-2 flush (5 hearts)
Flush beats straight — even if the opponent has AK for a straight, you still win
l1-basics-ex1.mistakeAction: Folding, thinking the opponent's straight is stronger
l1-basics-ex1.mistakeReasoning: Beginners often confuse the strength of flushes and straights. Remember: Flush > Straight!

l1-basics-ex2.title: Identify the hand: making a Full House
reasoning: You hold K♦K♣ and the board shows K♥7♦7♠
You make KKK77 — a full house (three Ks + a pair of 7s)
A full house is very strong — only beaten by four of a kind and straight flush
Bet big for value
l1-basics-ex2.mistakeAction: Checking, hoping to win at showdown
l1-basics-ex2.mistakeReasoning: With a full house you should actively bet for value instead of passively checking. Opponents may call with weaker hands.

l1-position-ex1.title: Same hand, different position: KJo in UTG vs BTN
reasoning: KJo in UTG is a marginal hand (right at the upper edge of the UTG opening range) — an open is loose; conservative play still suggests folding
Acting first means you have the least information, and 5 more players behind can raise
KJo is easily dominated (opponents may hold AK, KQ, AJ)
In early position, only the very strongest slice of hands gets played
l1-position-ex1.mistakeReasoning: KJo looks decent, but it's too weak in early position. If someone behind 3-Bets, you'll be in a very tough spot.

l1-position-ex2.title: Blind steal from BTN
reasoning: T8s on the BTN facing all folds is a standard open
The BTN is the widest opening position at a 6-max table (about 35% of hands)
Suited connectors play very well postflop
Only SB and BB remain — you may win the blinds outright
l1-position-ex2.mistakeReasoning: Folding T8s on the BTN facing all folds is too tight. This is the clearest spot for positional advantage — use it.

l1-hand-ex1.title: Marginal hand judgement: A5o in MP
reasoning: A5o should fold in MP
Even with an Ace, the kicker (5) is too weak
Offsuit has no flush potential and poor connectivity
Easily dominated (opponents may hold AQ, AJ, AT)
l1-hand-ex1.mistakeAction: Open-raising just because of the Ace
l1-hand-ex1.mistakeReasoning: Many beginners want to play any Ace, but A5o's kicker is too weak. If an opponent also has an Ace, you almost always lose.

l1-hand-ex2.title: The value of suited connectors: 98s in CO
reasoning: 98s in CO is a standard open
Suited connectors have great postflop playability
They can make straights, flushes, two pair, and more
From the CO the range can widen
l1-hand-ex2.mistakeReasoning: Suited connectors' value comes from connectivity and suitedness, not high cards. 98s in CO is a +EV open.
